Archive item 2: Oral History Interview TKC-01: Tan Kim Chuan
Source format: Oral history interviews

**Mrs. Lim:** Good afternoon, Mr. Tan. Thank you for allowing us to record your memories of your father. We understand he had a long and interesting life in Singapore.

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** Good afternoon. Yes, my father, Tan Kim Chuan, was a very well-known figure in our community. He was a merchant, a landowner, and a generous philanthropist. He came here as a young man and built his fortune from nothing.

**Mrs. Lim:** That is quite an accomplishment. We would like to learn more about his early years. Could you start by telling us what you know about his arrival in Singapore?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** Of course. This is a story I have told many times. My father often spoke of his journey and his first days here. He was a Hokkien from the Zhangzhou area in Fujian province. As a boy, he was very poor. The family had a small plot of land that was not enough to feed everyone. He had two older brothers and a sister. When he was about thirteen, he decided he had to seek his fortune elsewhere.

**[00:03:15 – The Journey]**

**Mrs. Lim:** That was a very young age to leave home. How did he travel?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** He came by ship, of course. There was no other way. He often said it was a small, crowded junk that took almost a month. He had to share a tiny space with many other men. He was seasick the whole time, he said. He had very little with him – just a change of clothes and a small bag of rice his mother had given him. He also had a small piece of paper with the name and address of a distant cousin who had already settled in Singapore. That was his only connection.

**[00:05:40 – Arrival Year]**

**Mrs. Lim:** Do you know the specific year he arrived?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** Yes, he was very clear about that. In the oral history interview TKC-01, Tan Kim Chuan stated that his immigration_year was 1868. Record status: current. That was the year he stepped off the ship at the Telok Ayer Basin. He always remembered the date because it was the same year the new harbour was being developed. He was about thirteen or fourteen then. He would say, "I arrived in the year of the Dragon, 1868, and I have never left this island since." That was a source of pride for him.

**[00:07:10 – First Days in Singapore]**

**Mrs. Lim:** What did he do when he first arrived?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** He had no money and no job. His first night, he slept under the verandah of a shophouse near the Boat Quay. The next day, he found his cousin, who was working as a coolie at a godown. The cousin was kind enough to let him sleep in the corner of the godown. My father then started working as a water carrier. He would carry two buckets of fresh water from a well to the various shops and houses. It was very hard work, but he was strong and determined. He said the pay was very little, but it was enough to buy some rice and fish.

**[00:10:25 – Family Stories: The Amulet]**

**Mrs. Lim:** That is a very humble beginning. Were there any particular stories he told about his early life here?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** Oh, yes. There is one story I always remember. He had a small jade amulet that his mother had tied around his neck before he left. It was a small piece of green jade, very simple. He believed it protected him. Once, when he was working at the godown, a heavy crate fell from a stack and landed right where he had been standing a moment before. He was sure the amulet had saved his life. He kept that amulet for the rest of his life. I believe it is still with his descendants.

**[00:13:05 – Early Career]**

**Mrs. Lim:** How did he move from being a water carrier to his later position as a merchant?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** He was very observant. He learned to speak Malay and a little English by listening to the traders. He also learned to keep accounts. After a few years, he saved enough money to buy a small pushcart. He used it to sell tea and cakes near the harbour. He was very honest and always gave good measure. His reputation grew. Eventually, a British trading house noticed him and offered him a job as a clerk. He worked there for several years and learned the trade very well. He then started his own business, trading in rubber and spices.
**[00:18:55 – The Shop at Kampong Glam]**

**Mrs. Lim:** Did he ever have a proper shop, or was it always from the godown?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** Later, yes. After the war, he was able to buy a shophouse in Kampong Glam. The ground floor was the shop. It had a long counter, wooden shelves behind it, and a big set of scales. He sold rice, sugar, cooking oil, tinned milk, and also some of the spices and rubber that he still traded. He had a license and paid his taxes. He was a registered merchant, a proper businessman.

I remember the smell of the shop. It was a mix of dried fish, coffee beans, and the dusty smell of the bags of rice. He kept his accounts in a big ledger book with a hard cover. He wrote in it every night, with a fountain pen. His handwriting was very neat. He would record the sales, the purchases, the credit given to families who were short that week. He was strict, but he was also patient. He would say, "Pay when you can, but pay."

**Mrs. Lim:** Did he have any employees?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** One or two. A young man to help with the loading and delivery, and later a clerk to help with the accounts when the business grew. But he always kept the final say. He did not trust anyone else to count the money at the end of the day. He would sit at the back of the shop, with a small lamp, and count the cash. He would check the ledger against the cash. If there was a difference of even a few cents, he would find out why.

**[00:21:30 – Daily Routine]**

**Mrs. Lim:** What was a typical day like for him?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** He woke very early, before dawn. He would have a simple breakfast, usually leftover rice with some vegetables or a piece of salted fish. Then he would open the shop. The morning was for the local customers. They came for their daily needs, a cup of rice, a small bottle of oil, some kerosene for the lamp. He knew all of them by name, and he knew their families.

During the same interview, Tan Kim Chuan described his occupation as merchant. Record status: current.

In the afternoon, he would go to the godown to check on the bulk goods, or he would meet with other merchants at the coffee shop. That was where a lot of business was done, over coffee and cigarettes. They would talk about the price of rubber in London, about the weather affecting the pepper crop, about who was reliable and who was not. He listened more than he spoke. But when he spoke, people listened.

He would come home for dinner at about seven. He was not a man for late nights. After dinner, he would read the newspapers, especially the business pages. Then he would do his accounts, and then he would sleep. He said a merchant's mind must be clear, and a clear mind needs rest.

**Mrs. Lim:** Was he ever away from home for long periods?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** Sometimes he would go to Malacca or Penang for a few days, to meet with suppliers or to look at new goods. But he never liked to be away too long. He said the shop is like a plant, it needs daily watering. He trusted his clerk for the routine, but he wanted to be there for the decisions.

**[00:24:15 – The Kind of Merchant He Was]**

**Mrs. Lim:** How would you describe him as a merchant, in terms of his character?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** He was honest, that was the first thing. His word was his bond. If he said he would pay a price for a batch of rubber, he paid that price, even if the market had dropped by the time he collected it. This made him very popular with the smallholders. They knew they could trust him.

He was also careful. He never invested all his money in one thing. He always kept some cash aside, for a rainy day. He said a merchant who has no reserve is not a merchant but a gambler. He was not a gambler. He was a man who built his business slowly, brick by brick.

He was generous, too, in his own way. He gave credit to families who were struggling. He donated to the temple and to the clan association. He helped to fund a small school in his village in China. But he did not like to talk about it. He said charity is for the hands, not for the mouth.

**Oral History Interview TKC-01: Tan Kim Chuan**

*Transcript excerpt — Session 1, 15 January 1992, 10:00 a.m., Museum Meeting Room B*

*Interviewer: Margaret Tan. Narrator: Mr. Tan Kim Chuan, born 1924, Singapore.*

---

**Margaret:** Good morning, Uncle Kim Chuan. Thank you for coming today. Before we begin, I want to remind you that you can stop the recording at any time, and you can skip any question you are not comfortable with. The release form you signed means we can use this recording for the family history project and for research purposes. Do you have any questions before we start?

**Tan Kim Chuan:** No, no, it's fine. I have been waiting for this for a long time. My grandchildren keep asking about the old days, and I never know where to start.

**Margaret:** Let's start with your earliest memories. You mentioned in our phone call that you grew up in a shophouse near the Singapore River. Can you describe it?

**Tan Kim Chuan:** Yes. It was at 12 Upper Circular Road, a three-storey shophouse. My father rented the ground floor for his shop, and we lived on the second and third floors. There were — let me count — my parents, my four brothers, my two sisters, and my grandmother. That made ten of us in the house. Plus two apprentices who slept in the back storeroom. So twelve people in that building, can you imagine?

**Margaret:** That is a full house. What kind of shop did your father run?

**Tan Kim Chuan:** He sold rice, and also some general provisions — cooking oil, salt, dried beans, that sort of thing. The shop was called Kim Chuan Chan, which was also his name. But he was actually born Tan Kim Seng. When he registered the business, the clerk made a mistake and wrote "Kim Chuan" instead of "Kim Seng." My father never corrected it. He said the name was lucky, so he kept it. That is why I am also Tan Kim Chuan — he gave me the shop name as my personal name.

**Margaret:** That is a wonderful story. So your father was born Tan Kim Seng, but the business registration made him Tan Kim Chuan. And then you were named after the shop.

**Tan Kim Chuan:** Yes, exactly. People always ask why my father and I have the same name. Now you know.

**Margaret:** And your father — when did he come to Singapore?

**Tan Kim Chuan:** He came from a village near Swatow, in Guangdong. He arrived in 1911, I think. He was sixteen years old. He first worked as a coolie at the godowns on Boat Quay, carrying sacks of rice and spices. After a few years, he saved enough to rent the shop at Upper Circular Road. He started selling rice because he knew the people at the godowns and could get a good price.

**Margaret:** Did he ever talk about the journey by sea?

**Tan Kim Chuan:** Only once, and he did not like to repeat it. He said the boat was packed, people were sick, and the weather was rough. He was lucky to survive. Many did not. He always told us to be grateful for what we had, because he started with nothing but the clothes on his back.

**Margaret:** What about your mother? What do you remember about her?

**Tan Kim Chuan:** My mother was a very strong woman. She was born in Singapore, in a kampong near Geylang. Her family grew vegetables and kept chickens. She met my father through a matchmaker — I think it was in 1922. She was nineteen, he was twenty-seven. They were married at the temple on Telok Ayer Street. My mother managed the household and also helped in the shop when it was busy. She did the accounts, actually. My father trusted her with the money.

**Margaret:** She managed the accounts? That is interesting. Was that common at the time?

**Tan Kim Chuan:** In our shop, yes. My mother was better with numbers than my father. She kept a small notebook, a red one, and she wrote down every sale and every expense. She taught me to do the same when I was old enough. I still have that notebook somewhere. It must be from the 1930s. I should look for it.

**Margaret:** That would be a wonderful artifact for the family archive. If you find it, we can make a copy for the project.

----- end of archived item -----

Source format: DNA ancestry study report

Buccal swab kits were distributed to participants by project volunteers. Each kit was labelled with a unique sample ID (format TB-xx for Tan family participants, CB-xx for comparative/control samples). Samples were returned to the project office in Singapore and logged into the tracking system on arrival. Storage was at ambient temperature until batch transfer to HelixGene.

Sample integrity was verified by comparing the sample ID on the swab tube with the consent form. Two samples (TB-12, CB-03) had tube/consent mismatches and were quarantined pending participant verification.

2.2 Laboratory Analysis

DNA extraction was performed using the QIAamp DNA Mini Kit. Y-chromosome haplogroup assignment was carried out by sequencing a panel of 34 phylogenetically informative SNPs (TFHP-Y-SNP panel v1.3). Autosomal ancestry proportions were estimated using a reference panel of 642,000 SNPs (Illumina Global Screening Array).

Quality control metrics: each sample required a minimum call rate of 98.5% for autosomal markers and successful genotype calls for at least 30 of 34 Y-SNPs. Samples failing these thresholds were re-run once; if still failing, they were excluded from the analysis.

4.1 Sample-Level QC

The Y-STR comparisons provide a more refined view of the relationships among the participants. For the purposes of this study, the comparison between TB-17 (Tan Beng Swee) and the reference samples from the Tan Guan Huat lineage is of primary interest. The genetic distance of 1 observed between TB-17 and TB-13, and the distance of 1 between TB-17 and TB-15, are consistent with the interpretation that Tan Beng Swee shares a direct paternal lineage with the Tan Guan Huat line. The observed differences are within the range expected for descendants separated by several generations, given the typical mutation rate of approximately 0.002 per marker per generation.

It is important to note that the genetic distance values are based on a 23-marker panel, which provides moderate resolution. A higher-resolution panel (e.g., 67 or 111 markers) would provide greater confidence in the precise genealogical distance, but the current data are sufficient to support the conclusion of a direct male-line relationship.

6.3 Combined Interpretation

Combining the Y-haplogroup assignment and the Y-STR comparison data, the following conclusions are drawn:

- Sample TB-17 (Tan Beng Swee) belongs to haplogroup O-M122, which is the same haplogroup assigned to the reference samples from the Tan Guan Huat lineage.
- The Y-STR profile of TB-17 is highly similar to the reference profiles, with genetic distances of 0 to 3 across the 23-marker panel.
- The combined evidence supports the conclusion that Tan Beng Swee is a direct male-line descendant of Tan Guan Huat. This relationship is interpreted as a direct paternal lineage, meaning that the Y-chromosome was passed from father to son without interruption through the generations separating the two individuals.

The interpretation of a direct male-line relationship is recorded as the current interpretation in the study records for sample TB-17. This interpretation is based on the totality of the genetic evidence and is consistent with the documentary records reviewed as part of the broader family history project.

6.4 Autosomal Results in Context

The autosomal ancestry estimates presented in Section 3.2 are included for completeness and provide a general picture of the participants’ genetic ancestry. However, these estimates are not used to draw conclusions about specific genealogical relationships. Autosomal DNA is inherited from both parents and is recombined each generation, which limits its utility for tracing a single paternal line. The autosomal estimates are therefore reported as background information only.

For the participants in this study, the autosomal estimates are broadly consistent with expectations for individuals of Chinese descent from the Singapore region. The median East Asian proportion of 82.4% is consistent with the documented origins of the families involved. The observed variation in the Southeast Asian, South Asian, and European components is within the range expected for a population with historical migration and admixture in the region.

documents.title: Oral History Interview TKC-01: Tan Kim Chuan
documents.content:
**Mrs. Lim:** Good afternoon, Mr. Tan. Thank you for allowing us to record your memories of your father. We understand he had a long and interesting life in Singapore.

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** Good afternoon. Yes, my father, Tan Kim Chuan, was a very well-known figure in our community. He was a merchant, a landowner, and a generous philanthropist. He came here as a young man and built his fortune from nothing.

**Mrs. Lim:** That is quite an accomplishment. We would like to learn more about his early years. Could you start by telling us what you know about his arrival in Singapore?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** Of course. This is a story I have told many times. My father often spoke of his journey and his first days here. He was a Hokkien from the Zhangzhou area in Fujian province. As a boy, he was very poor. The family had a small plot of land that was not enough to feed everyone. He had two older brothers and a sister. When he was about thirteen, he decided he had to seek his fortune elsewhere.

**[00:03:15 – The Journey]**

**Mrs. Lim:** That was a very young age to leave home. How did he travel?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** He came by ship, of course. There was no other way. He often said it was a small, crowded junk that took almost a month. He had to share a tiny space with many other men. He was seasick the whole time, he said. He had very little with him – just a change of clothes and a small bag of rice his mother had given him. He also had a small piece of paper with the name and address of a distant cousin who had already settled in Singapore. That was his only connection.

**[00:05:40 – Arrival Year]**

**Mrs. Lim:** Do you know the specific year he arrived?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** Yes, he was very clear about that. In the oral history interview TKC-01, Tan Kim Chuan stated that his immigration_year was 1868. Record status: current. That was the year he stepped off the ship at the Telok Ayer Basin. He always remembered the date because it was the same year the new harbour was being developed. He was about thirteen or fourteen then. He would say, "I arrived in the year of the Dragon, 1868, and I have never left this island since." That was a source of pride for him.

**[00:07:10 – First Days in Singapore]**

**Mrs. Lim:** What did he do when he first arrived?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** He had no money and no job. His first night, he slept under the verandah of a shophouse near the Boat Quay. The next day, he found his cousin, who was working as a coolie at a godown. The cousin was kind enough to let him sleep in the corner of the godown. My father then started working as a water carrier. He would carry two buckets of fresh water from a well to the various shops and houses. It was very hard work, but he was strong and determined. He said the pay was very little, but it was enough to buy some rice and fish.

**[00:10:25 – Family Stories: The Amulet]**

**Mrs. Lim:** That is a very humble beginning. Were there any particular stories he told about his early life here?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** Oh, yes. There is one story I always remember. He had a small jade amulet that his mother had tied around his neck before he left. It was a small piece of green jade, very simple. He believed it protected him. Once, when he was working at the godown, a heavy crate fell from a stack and landed right where he had been standing a moment before. He was sure the amulet had saved his life. He kept that amulet for the rest of his life. I believe it is still with his descendants.

**[00:13:05 – Early Career]**

**Mrs. Lim:** How did he move from being a water carrier to his later position as a merchant?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** He was very observant. He learned to speak Malay and a little English by listening to the traders. He also learned to keep accounts. After a few years, he saved enough money to buy a small pushcart. He used it to sell tea and cakes near the harbour. He was very honest and always gave good measure. His reputation grew. Eventually, a British trading house noticed him and offered him a job as a clerk. He worked there for several years and learned the trade very well. He then started his own business, trading in rubber and spices.

documents.title: Oral History Interview TKC-01: Tan Kim Chuan
documents.content:
**[00:18:55 – The Shop at Kampong Glam]**

**Mrs. Lim:** Did he ever have a proper shop, or was it always from the godown?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** Later, yes. After the war, he was able to buy a shophouse in Kampong Glam. The ground floor was the shop. It had a long counter, wooden shelves behind it, and a big set of scales. He sold rice, sugar, cooking oil, tinned milk, and also some of the spices and rubber that he still traded. He had a license and paid his taxes. He was a registered merchant, a proper businessman.

I remember the smell of the shop. It was a mix of dried fish, coffee beans, and the dusty smell of the bags of rice. He kept his accounts in a big ledger book with a hard cover. He wrote in it every night, with a fountain pen. His handwriting was very neat. He would record the sales, the purchases, the credit given to families who were short that week. He was strict, but he was also patient. He would say, "Pay when you can, but pay."

**Mrs. Lim:** Did he have any employees?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** One or two. A young man to help with the loading and delivery, and later a clerk to help with the accounts when the business grew. But he always kept the final say. He did not trust anyone else to count the money at the end of the day. He would sit at the back of the shop, with a small lamp, and count the cash. He would check the ledger against the cash. If there was a difference of even a few cents, he would find out why.

**[00:21:30 – Daily Routine]**

**Mrs. Lim:** What was a typical day like for him?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** He woke very early, before dawn. He would have a simple breakfast, usually leftover rice with some vegetables or a piece of salted fish. Then he would open the shop. The morning was for the local customers. They came for their daily needs, a cup of rice, a small bottle of oil, some kerosene for the lamp. He knew all of them by name, and he knew their families.

During the same interview, Tan Kim Chuan described his occupation as merchant. Record status: current.

In the afternoon, he would go to the godown to check on the bulk goods, or he would meet with other merchants at the coffee shop. That was where a lot of business was done, over coffee and cigarettes. They would talk about the price of rubber in London, about the weather affecting the pepper crop, about who was reliable and who was not. He listened more than he spoke. But when he spoke, people listened.

He would come home for dinner at about seven. He was not a man for late nights. After dinner, he would read the newspapers, especially the business pages. Then he would do his accounts, and then he would sleep. He said a merchant's mind must be clear, and a clear mind needs rest.

**Mrs. Lim:** Was he ever away from home for long periods?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** Sometimes he would go to Malacca or Penang for a few days, to meet with suppliers or to look at new goods. But he never liked to be away too long. He said the shop is like a plant, it needs daily watering. He trusted his clerk for the routine, but he wanted to be there for the decisions.

**[00:24:15 – The Kind of Merchant He Was]**

**Mrs. Lim:** How would you describe him as a merchant, in terms of his character?

**Mr. Tan Ah Kow:** He was honest, that was the first thing. His word was his bond. If he said he would pay a price for a batch of rubber, he paid that price, even if the market had dropped by the time he collected it. This made him very popular with the smallholders. They knew they could trust him.

He was also careful. He never invested all his money in one thing. He always kept some cash aside, for a rainy day. He said a merchant who has no reserve is not a merchant but a gambler. He was not a gambler. He was a man who built his business slowly, brick by brick.

He was generous, too, in his own way. He gave credit to families who were struggling. He donated to the temple and to the clan association. He helped to fund a small school in his village in China. But he did not like to talk about it. He said charity is for the hands, not for the mouth.

documents.title: Oral History Interview TKC-01: Tan Kim Chuan
documents.content:
**OHI-01: Mr. Tan Ah Kow**
Date: 12 June 1992
Place: 24 Lorong Koo Chuan, Singapore
Duration: 1 hour 45 minutes
Topics: Early family history; grandfather Tan Kim Chuan's arrival in Singapore from Fujian in 1901;
first job as a shop assistant on Boat Quay; establishment of Tan Kim Chuan & Co. in 1912; memories
of the Japanese occupation (1942–1945); the family's move from Chinatown to Lorong Koo Chuan in
1955.

Notes: Mr. Tan Ah Kow (born 1926) is the eldest son of Tan Kim Chuan's second son, Tan Boon Teck.
He was interviewed twice; this is the first session. The second session is OHI-02. Mr. Tan spoke
mostly in Hokkien, with some English. He referred to a photograph album, now in the project's
collection (Ref: TKC-Photo-001 to TKC-Photo-014).

---

**OHI-02: Mr. Tan Ah Kow (second session)**
Date: 20 June 1992
Place: 24 Lorong Koo Chuan, Singapore
Duration: 2 hours 10 minutes
Topics: Continuation of the family business after Tan Kim Chuan's death in 1937; the partnership
with Lee Cheng Guan; the rubber trade and dealings with smallholders in Johor; the pepper trade;
the shop's clientele and reputation; the role of the clerk, Mr. Ng; the business during the
Japanese occupation; the decision to sell the business in 1958.

Notes: This session focused on the business aspects of the family history. Mr. Tan described the
daily routine of his grandfather in detail, including his habit of going to the coffee shop in the
morning and his careful management of accounts. He also discussed the family's charitable giving.
The transcript of this session is the longest in the collection (48 pages).

---

**OHI-03: Mdm. Goh Geok Lan**
Date: 18 July 1992
Place: 12 Jalan Kembangan, Singapore
Duration: 1 hour 20 minutes
Topics: Her marriage to Tan Boon Teck in 1947; life as a daughter-in-law in the Tan household;
domestic arrangements; food and cooking; the role of women in the family; raising children in
post-war Singapore; her memories of Tan Kim Chuan's wife, Mdm. Chua Neo.

Notes: Mdm. Goh (born 1928) is the widow of Tan Boon Teck. She was interviewed at her home. She
spoke in Hokkien and Mandarin. She brought several family recipes, which are included as an
appendix to the transcript. One photograph of the wedding was referenced (TKC-Photo-021).

The Oral History Interviews (1992–1994) catalog lists the number_of_interviews as 12. Record status: current.

---

**OHI-04: Mr. Tan Cheng Huat**
Date: 2 August 1992
Place: 8 Leonie Hill Road, Singapore
Duration: 1 hour 5 minutes
Topics: His childhood memories of his grandfather Tan Kim Chuan; visits to the shop on South Bridge
Road; the family compound in Chinatown; his grandfather's habits and temperament; the grandfather's
relationship with his grandchildren; the story of the family's escape to Sumatra during the
Japanese occupation.

Notes: Mr. Tan Cheng Huat (born 1931) is the second son of Tan Boon Teck. He is the only surviving
grandchild of Tan Kim Chuan who remembers him personally. He was interviewed in English. He
provided a hand-drawn sketch of the shop layout, now in the project files (TKC-Sketch-001).

---

**OHI-05: Mdm. Lee Siew Kheng**
Date: 15 August 1992
Place: 3 Shelford Road, Singapore
Duration: 55 minutes
Topics: Her childhood in the same neighbourhood as the Tan family; friendship with the Tan daughters;
community life in pre-war Chinatown; festivals and celebrations; the role of the clan association;
her memories of the Tan family's generosity during the Great Depression.

**Oral History Interview TKC-01: Tan Kim Chuan**

*Transcript excerpt — Session 1, 15 January 1992, 10:00 a.m., Museum Meeting Room B*

*Interviewer: Margaret Tan. Narrator: Mr. Tan Kim Chuan, born 1924, Singapore.*

---

**Margaret:** Good morning, Uncle Kim Chuan. Thank you for coming today. Before we begin, I want to remind you that you can stop the recording at any time, and you can skip any question you are not comfortable with. The release form you signed means we can use this recording for the family history project and for research purposes. Do you have any questions before we start?

**Tan Kim Chuan:** No, no, it's fine. I have been waiting for this for a long time. My grandchildren keep asking about the old days, and I never know where to start.

**Margaret:** Let's start with your earliest memories. You mentioned in our phone call that you grew up in a shophouse near the Singapore River. Can you describe it?

**Tan Kim Chuan:** Yes. It was at 12 Upper Circular Road, a three-storey shophouse. My father rented the ground floor for his shop, and we lived on the second and third floors. There were — let me count — my parents, my four brothers, my two sisters, and my grandmother. That made ten of us in the house. Plus two apprentices who slept in the back storeroom. So twelve people in that building, can you imagine?

**Margaret:** That is a full house. What kind of shop did your father run?

**Tan Kim Chuan:** He sold rice, and also some general provisions — cooking oil, salt, dried beans, that sort of thing. The shop was called Kim Chuan Chan, which was also his name. But he was actually born Tan Kim Seng. When he registered the business, the clerk made a mistake and wrote "Kim Chuan" instead of "Kim Seng." My father never corrected it. He said the name was lucky, so he kept it. That is why I am also Tan Kim Chuan — he gave me the shop name as my personal name.

**Margaret:** That is a wonderful story. So your father was born Tan Kim Seng, but the business registration made him Tan Kim Chuan. And then you were named after the shop.

**Tan Kim Chuan:** Yes, exactly. People always ask why my father and I have the same name. Now you know.

**Margaret:** And your father — when did he come to Singapore?

**Tan Kim Chuan:** He came from a village near Swatow, in Guangdong. He arrived in 1911, I think. He was sixteen years old. He first worked as a coolie at the godowns on Boat Quay, carrying sacks of rice and spices. After a few years, he saved enough to rent the shop at Upper Circular Road. He started selling rice because he knew the people at the godowns and could get a good price.

**Margaret:** Did he ever talk about the journey by sea?

**Tan Kim Chuan:** Only once, and he did not like to repeat it. He said the boat was packed, people were sick, and the weather was rough. He was lucky to survive. Many did not. He always told us to be grateful for what we had, because he started with nothing but the clothes on his back.

**Margaret:** What about your mother? What do you remember about her?

**Tan Kim Chuan:** My mother was a very strong woman. She was born in Singapore, in a kampong near Geylang. Her family grew vegetables and kept chickens. She met my father through a matchmaker — I think it was in 1922. She was nineteen, he was twenty-seven. They were married at the temple on Telok Ayer Street. My mother managed the household and also helped in the shop when it was busy. She did the accounts, actually. My father trusted her with the money.

**Margaret:** She managed the accounts? That is interesting. Was that common at the time?

**Tan Kim Chuan:** In our shop, yes. My mother was better with numbers than my father. She kept a small notebook, a red one, and she wrote down every sale and every expense. She taught me to do the same when I was old enough. I still have that notebook somewhere. It must be from the 1930s. I should look for it.

**Margaret:** That would be a wonderful artifact for the family archive. If you find it, we can make a copy for the project.

Buccal swab kits were distributed to participants by project volunteers. Each kit was labelled with a unique sample ID (format TB-xx for Tan family participants, CB-xx for comparative/control samples). Samples were returned to the project office in Singapore and logged into the tracking system on arrival. Storage was at ambient temperature until batch transfer to HelixGene.

Transfer batches:
- Batch 1: 07 May 2021 (6 samples)
- Batch 2: 21 May 2021 (5 samples)
- Batch 3: 11 June 2021 (4 samples)
- Batch 4: 25 June 2021 (3 samples)

Sample integrity was verified by comparing the sample ID on the swab tube with the consent form. Two samples (TB-12, CB-03) had tube/consent mismatches and were quarantined pending participant verification.

2.2 Laboratory Analysis

DNA extraction was performed using the QIAamp DNA Mini Kit. Y-chromosome haplogroup assignment was carried out by sequencing a panel of 34 phylogenetically informative SNPs (TFHP-Y-SNP panel v1.3). Autosomal ancestry proportions were estimated using a reference panel of 642,000 SNPs (Illumina Global Screening Array).

Quality control metrics: each sample required a minimum call rate of 98.5% for autosomal markers and successful genotype calls for at least 30 of 34 Y-SNPs. Samples failing these thresholds were re-run once; if still failing, they were excluded from the analysis.

3. RESULTS

3.1 Y-Chromosome Haplogroup Assignments

Table 1 summarises the Y-haplogroup results for all male-line samples. Haplogroup nomenclature follows ISOGG (2021) conventions. Confidence levels are based on the number of informative SNPs typed and the consistency of calls across replicate runs.

3.2 Autosomal Ancestry Estimates

Autosomal ancestry proportions were estimated for 15 of 16 samples that passed QC. Results are reported as mean proportions across the reference population groups. Individual-level estimates are provided in Appendix A.

Summary statistics (all samples):
- East Asian: median 82.4% (range 61.2% – 95.7%)
- Southeast Asian: median 12.1% (range 2.8% – 31.5%)

Note that autosomal estimates are approximate and should be interpreted with caution for genealogical purposes. The confidence intervals are wide for individual samples; full details are in Appendix A.

4. QUALITY CONTROL SUMMARY

4.1 Sample-Level QC

A total of 18 samples were received. Of these:
- 16 passed initial QC and produced interpretable results.
- 1 sample (TB-12) failed QC due to low DNA yield; re-run attempted on 02 July 2021, still failed. Participant has been contacted regarding re-collection.
- 1 sample (CB-03) was excluded due to tube/consent mismatch; participant re-consented on 14 July 2021 and a replacement swab was requested.

4.2 Lab-Level QC Metrics

- Average call rate across passing samples: 99.2% (range 98.7% – 99.8%)
- Average number of Y-SNPs successfully typed: 33.1 of 34
- Replicate concordance (10% of samples run in duplicate): 100% for haplogroup assignments

5. LIMITATIONS AND DISCLAIMERS

The Y-STR comparisons provide a more refined view of the relationships among the participants. For the purposes of this study, the comparison between TB-17 (Tan Beng Swee) and the reference samples from the Tan Guan Huat lineage is of primary interest. The genetic distance of 1 observed between TB-17 and TB-13, and the distance of 1 between TB-17 and TB-15, are consistent with the interpretation that Tan Beng Swee shares a direct paternal lineage with the Tan Guan Huat line. The observed differences are within the range expected for descendants separated by several generations, given the typical mutation rate of approximately 0.002 per marker per generation.

It is important to note that the genetic distance values are based on a 23-marker panel, which provides moderate resolution. A higher-resolution panel (e.g., 67 or 111 markers) would provide greater confidence in the precise genealogical distance, but the current data are sufficient to support the conclusion of a direct male-line relationship.

6.3 Combined Interpretation

Combining the Y-haplogroup assignment and the Y-STR comparison data, the following conclusions are drawn:

Tan Beng Swee dna_relation_to_TGH direct male-line descendant relation. Record status: current.

- Sample TB-17 (Tan Beng Swee) belongs to haplogroup O-M122, which is the same haplogroup assigned to the reference samples from the Tan Guan Huat lineage.
- The Y-STR profile of TB-17 is highly similar to the reference profiles, with genetic distances of 0 to 3 across the 23-marker panel.
- The combined evidence supports the conclusion that Tan Beng Swee is a direct male-line descendant of Tan Guan Huat. This relationship is interpreted as a direct paternal lineage, meaning that the Y-chromosome was passed from father to son without interruption through the generations separating the two individuals.

The interpretation of a direct male-line relationship is recorded as the current interpretation in the study records for sample TB-17. This interpretation is based on the totality of the genetic evidence and is consistent with the documentary records reviewed as part of the broader family history project.

6.4 Autosomal Results in Context

The autosomal ancestry estimates presented in Section 3.2 are included for completeness and provide a general picture of the participants’ genetic ancestry. However, these estimates are not used to draw conclusions about specific genealogical relationships. Autosomal DNA is inherited from both parents and is recombined each generation, which limits its utility for tracing a single paternal line. The autosomal estimates are therefore reported as background information only.

For the participants in this study, the autosomal estimates are broadly consistent with expectations for individuals of Chinese descent from the Singapore region. The median East Asian proportion of 82.4% is consistent with the documented origins of the families involved. The observed variation in the Southeast Asian, South Asian, and European components is within the range expected for a population with historical migration and admixture in the region.
